Why your call sheet matters so much
Know exactly what you're asking for
Three ways to get your call sheet
call-sheet-instructions.text:
Your Call Sheet — LeskoHelp
?
?
?
Lesko
Help
Call Sheets · Getting Started
Your call sheet is your 
treasure map
 to 
free money.
It's the list of places you can contact to find grants — built around where you live and the problem you need help with. This page explains what it is, why it matters, and the three ways to get yours. 💛
Join a Call Sheet Class →
📋
What a call sheet is
A call sheet is a list of the organizations you can contact to find grants — with the address and phone number for each one.
Every call sheet is built around 
two things
:
✔
Where you live
 — your ZIP code, and your state or city.
✔
Your problem
 — the one thing you need help with.
Put those together and you get a list of real places, with real phone numbers, that help people in your situation.
⭐
Why your call sheet matters so much
Almost everything else you do here starts with your call sheet. Without one, there's nobody to call.
✔
It's built for you.
 Not a general list from the internet — your ZIP code, your state, your problem.
✔
Help is local.
 Most of this money is handed out county by county. That's why your ZIP code matters so much.
✔
It turns "I don't know where to start" into a list.
 That's the hardest part, solved.
💰
A lot of this money is never advertised. It sits quietly with local offices and organizations who give it to the people who contact them and ask.
☝️
One problem = one call sheet
Always make a separate list for each problem. Never try to combine several problems into one list.
Do this — a separate sheet for each
"Help paying rent" · "Car repair help" · "Help with medical bills"
✔ Each list is full of organizations that really do that one thing.
Not this — everything in one
"Rent, my car and my medical bills"
✖ You get a thin, general list — and you won't know who to call about what.
💛
More than one problem? Wonderful.
 Just ask for more than one call sheet. There's no limit.
🎯
Know exactly what you're asking for
Before you join a class or ask your question, be really sure about the problem you want help with. The clearer you are, the better your call sheet will be.
If you're not sure yet, these questions will help you find it:
01
What is the 
one problem
 you most need help with right now?
02
If someone handed you the money tomorrow, 
what exactly would it pay for?
03
What 
bill is keeping you up at night?
04
What do you keep 
saying no to
 because you can't afford it?
05
Is this for 
you, your family, or your business?
06
Are you a 
veteran, a senior, disabled, a single parent, a caregiver, a student?
 Say so — each one opens doors that others can't use.
07
What is your 
ZIP code
, and your 
state or city
?
📝
Bring three things with you:
 your problem in one sentence, your ZIP code, and your state. That's exactly what the team writes down when they make your call sheet.
🗺️
Three ways to get your call sheet
These aren't either-or. 
Try all three
 — each one gives you something the others don't.
1
Join a Call Sheet Class
The team shows you how call sheets are made and how to use them — and if there's time after class, they'll make one for you. The AI Workshops cover this too.
Join a class →
2
Make one with the Lesko AI Researcher
Our own AI app. Give it your problem and your ZIP code, and it builds your call sheet for you.
Try the AI →
3
Ask in the Questions Channel
Post your problem with your state and ZIP code, and the team makes your call sheet and posts it back to you.
Ask a question →
⭐
Please try all three.
 Members who use every route end up with the best lists — and you'll pick up something new each time.
🙋
Asking for your call sheet
Whether you ask in a class or in the Questions Channel, two things keep you safe and get you a better answer.
🔒
Never share anything personal.
 No phone number, no email address, no home address — nothing that could identify you. Classes and the Questions Channel can be seen by other members.
✔
Be as precise as you can about the problem itself.
 Your ZIP code, your state and what you need are safe to share — and they're all anyone needs.
Precise, and identifies nobody
"I'm a disabled veteran in ZIP 43604 and I need help paying my rent."
🤗
Please don't be shy — show up and ask.
 Everyone there needed help too, and nobody is judging you. If you'd rather not be recognised, use an 
avatar picture and a different name
, keep your camera off, and type in the chat. You get exactly the same help. 💛
🔖
Always bookmark your question.
 Hover over your post and click the little 
bookmark sign 🔖
 at the top right. You'll find it again under your personal settings, in 
Bookmarked Posts
 — so you never lose your answer. You can ask as many questions as you like.
There's more about writing a good question inside the Questions Channel itself.
🔁
Keep going
One call sheet is a start. The members who do best are the ones who come back again and again.
✔
A sheet for every problem.
 Three problems, three sheets.
✔
Come back to the classes.
 Every coach has a different angle, and other members' questions turn up things you'd never have thought to ask.
✔
Ask again whenever something changes.
 New problem, new sheet.
♾️
There's no limit
 — not on call sheets, not on classes, not on questions. Use all of it, as often as you like.
🤖
A note about AI.
 AI can make mistakes. Sometimes a name or a phone number on a call sheet isn't quite right. If something looks wrong or you're not sure about it, please 
join one of our classes and ask a grant coach
 — they'll help you get the right information lined up. That's exactly what they're there for. 💛
Join a Call Sheet Class →
Ask in the Questions Channel →
Ask the AI →
"My joy is helping people find money programs that make life a little easier." — Matthew Lesko
↑

application-follow-up.text:
After You Apply — LeskoHelp
?
?
?
Lesko
Help
Grant Hunt · After You Apply
You've applied. 
Now comes
the part that wins.
Most people send their application and then go quiet. The members who actually get the money are the ones who stay organised, stay reachable, and follow up at the right moment. Here's how. 💛
Bring it to a Group Coaching class →
🧘
First — stay calm. This part is slow.
Waiting is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It's just how these offices work.
✔
Most decisions take 30 to 60 days.
 Some take longer. Silence in week two means nothing at all.
✔
A "no" is usually about their budget, not about you.
 Funds run out, windows close, rules shift. It isn't a judgement on you.
✔
Most refusals come from missing paperwork
 — not from the person being undeserving. That part you can control, and this page is about exactly that.
💛
You are allowed to find this stressful. Come to a class and say so — you'll find a room full of people going through the very same thing.
📁
Keep a dossier — one folder per application
Not one big pile. 
One folder for each thing you applied to
, named for the organization. Paper in a real folder, or digital on your computer — whichever you'll actually keep up.
📂 Toledo Housing Fund — applied 12 Aug
A copy of the application exactly as you sent it
Every document you attached — bills, proof of income, ID
Proof you sent it — the email, the receipt, the confirmation number
Every letter or email they send back
Your notes page: dates, names, what was said
📸
Never send your only copy.
 Photograph or scan every page before it leaves your hands. If they lose something — and it happens — you can send it again the same day instead of starting over.
💡
Name your files with the date.
2026-08-12 housing-fund application.pdf
 sorts itself in order and you'll never hunt for the right version.
🗓️
Write down every date and every name
This is the single most useful habit on this page. Every time you speak to anyone, write four things down.
1
The date
 you called or wrote.
2
The name
 of the person you spoke to — and their direct number or extension.
3
What they told you
 in one line.
4
When to check back
 — the date they gave you, or the one you chose.
Date
Who
What they said
Check back
12 Aug
—
Applied online, ref #4471
19 Aug
19 Aug
Denise, x214
Received, in review, 30 days
18 Sep
02 Sep
Denise, x214
Needs last 2 utility bills
03 Sep — send!
03 Sep
—
Bills emailed, got read receipt
18 Sep
🗣️
A name changes everything.
 "I spoke with Denise on the 19th, extension 214" gets you straight to the person who knows your file — instead of explaining your whole story to a stranger again.
❓
Always end a call with one question:
"When should I check back with you?"
 Then use that exact date. Now you're following their timetable, not guessing.
⏰
When to follow up — and how often
There is a rhythm to this. Too soon and you're a nuisance; too late and your file goes quiet. This is a sensible pattern to follow.
DAY 0
You apply
Write the date in your folder. Save the confirmation.
DAY 3–5
One short call to confirm it arrived
"I'm just checking my application arrived safely." That's all. Ask how long a decision usually takes, and who is handling it.
THEN WAIT
Let their window run
Whatever they told you — 30 days, 6 weeks — leave them alone until it's up. Calling every few days does not speed anything up, and it's remembered.
EVERY 2 WKS
After the window, a polite check-in
Once every couple of weeks. Short and friendly: your name, your reference number, "is there anything you still need from me?"
SAME DAY
If they ask you for anything — drop everything
See the next card. This is the one deadline you cannot miss.
🤝
No deadline given? Assume 30 days,
 then start your two-week check-ins. And always ask for a date rather than guessing one.
😊
Be the applicant they like hearing from.
 Short, friendly, organised, never cross. The person on the phone often has some say in what happens next — and they remember who was kind.
⚡
If they ask for more — drop everything
A request for extra information is 
good news
 — it means someone is actually looking at your file. It also comes with the shortest deadline you'll meet, sometimes as little as ten days.
🚨
A late or half-finished reply is usually an automatic no.
 Not a delay — a refusal. This is where most applications quietly die, and it is completely avoidable.
✔
Answer within days, not weeks.
 Don't sit on it until the deadline.
✔
Send everything they asked for in one go.
 Piece by piece causes confusion and delay. If they listed five things, send five things.
✔
Read the letter twice
 before you reply, so you don't miss the small request buried in the last line.
✔
Keep a copy of what you sent, and proof you sent it.
 A read receipt, a confirmation email, or a postal receipt.
✔
Then call to confirm it arrived
 — and write down who you spoke to.
🙋
Don't understand what they're asking for? Ask us.
 Bring the letter to a Group Coaching class and a grant coach will help you read it. Far better than guessing and getting it wrong.
📬
Check your messages every single day
You can do everything else right and still lose a grant because a letter sat unopened for two weeks. Make this a daily habit while you have applications out.
✔
Your email — including the spam folder.
 Official mail lands in spam constantly. Check it every day.
✔
Your letterbox.
 A lot of these offices still write on paper.
✔
Your voicemail.
 Make sure it's set up, and that it isn't full — a full mailbox means they simply can't reach you.
✔
Answer numbers you don't recognise
 while you're waiting. It's often them.
✔
Your posts here in the community,
 so you see it when a coach replies to you.
📞
Did your phone number or address change?
 Tell every organization you've applied to, straight away. Otherwise the good news goes to the wrong place.
🎓
Group Coaching — bring it to a class
You don't have to work any of this out alone. All our live help sits together under 
Group Coaching
 — three kinds of class, one place to find them.
1
Q&A
Built for one thing: answering your questions. Bring what's unclear or wherever you're stuck. Some sessions focus on 
paying bills and debt
.
2
Drop-In Clinic
Thursdays, open almost all day, with several grant coaches there. Hop in whenever suits you — no appointment needed. The best place to bring a letter you don't understand.
3
Open Office
The bigger picture — what to do next, how to keep moving, how to find your way around. Come here when you're unsure what your next step should be.
See all Group Coaching classes →
🙌
Hop into a class as often as you can
 — there's no limit. And don't just wait for your own turn: 
other members' questions are often the most useful part
. You'll hear answers to things you'd never have thought to ask.
▶️
Missed one? Watch the replay.
 Every class is recorded, so a time that didn't suit you is never a class lost.
🔖
Or ask in the Questions Channel
 any time — day or night, as many questions as you like. Bookmark your post so you can find the answer again, and never put personal details like your phone number, address or account numbers in a post.
Ask in the Questions Channel →
📰
Keep hunting while you wait
Waiting on one answer is no reason to stop. The members who do best always have several applications out at once.
✔
New programs open all the time.
 Check the Grant News for anything you could apply for today.
✔
Watch Matthew's latest videos.
 He's forever turning up programs most people have never heard of.
✔
Every "no" has a next date.
 A program with no money this month may have a new budget next quarter — ask when to try again, and put it in your folder.
Latest Grant News →
Matthew's latest videos →
🤖
A note about AI.
 AI can make mistakes — a name, a phone number, or a deadline may not be right. Always check anything important against the organization's own letter or website, and if something looks wrong or you're unsure, bring it to a grant coach in one of our classes. That's exactly what they're there for. 💛
Join a Group Coaching class →
Ask in the Questions Channel →
Latest Grant News →

Common questions
Things people ask before joining.
Are these actually real grants? It feels too good.
+
Yes. Every program in our database is a real, government or foundation-administered grant. Matthew has been cataloging them for 50 years. The catch isn't that they don't exist. It's that they're scattered across thousands of agencies, foundations, and state programs that don't market themselves. Our job is to surface the ones you qualify for.
I'm a freelancer or a one-person business. Do grants even apply to me?
+
More than you'd expect. There are programs specifically for sole proprietors, individual artists, freelance researchers, women-owned businesses, veteran-owned businesses, rural entrepreneurs, and many other niches. The AI report is built to find the ones that match your specific situation, not just generic small-business programs.
How is this different from just searching Grants.gov myself?
+
Grants.gov is one source: the federal one. Most of the funding for small operators actually comes from state agencies, regional economic development offices, and private foundations that aren't on Grants.gov at all. Our database covers all of those, and the coaching helps you actually navigate the application, not just find it.
Will someone write my grant application for me?
+
No, and that's intentional. Grant writers cost $2,000–$10,000+ per application and can't fund themselves working on a freelance budget. We coach you through writing your own, with feedback at every step. Most members find that after one or two applications, they can do it themselves with confidence.
What if I'm too busy to attend live classes?
+
Classes run every weekday across multiple time zones, and most are recorded. Many members never attend live. They post in the Questions Channel and get replies within hours. The community works asynchronously too.
Is this U.S. only?
+
Yes — LeskoHelp Pro is U.S. only. The database covers federal, state, local, and U.S. foundation programs, and they're available to everyone in America. Some programs don't even require you to be a citizen.
What's the refund policy?
+
30-day money-back guarantee on all plans. If you join, attend a few classes, generate a report, and decide it's not for you, we refund you. No forms, no friction.
